29048-the-fabric-of-civilization-a-short:
The Guaranty Trust Company of New York published this 1919 survey, The Fabric of Civilization, on the cotton industry in the United States. The survey aims to give general facts in brief compass, not to cover every corner of the field, so a reader can quickly learn the industry's broader outlines. A cotton price chart, showing spot prices for middling uplands in New York, fronts the book.

Chapters treat the importance and power of cotton, where it is grown and spun, the raw cotton market, the cloth market, and financing. Later chapters cover American cloth abroad, the grower's problems, the mill, and finishing operations. Readers get a banker's clear survey of an industry that touched most lives on earth, built peoples, and sometimes tore them apart.
31891-essays-on-the-constitution-of-the-:
Paul Leicester Ford's 1892 collection Essays on the Constitution of the United States, published during its discussion by the people in 1787 and 1788, gathers the pamphlet arguments of ratification. Ford had earlier selected fourteen tracts for his Pamphlets on the Constitution, and this volume extends that work.

Its contents include the letters of Cassius by James Sullivan, Agrippa accredited to James Winthrop. They also include the Landholder letters of Oliver Ellsworth, Cato by George Clinton, Caesar by Alexander Hamilton, Sydney by Robert Yates, and a letter of caution by Samuel Chase. Readers get the ratification debate in the voices of its participants, Federalist and Anti-Federalist alike.
34123-familiar-letters-of-john-adams-and:
Charles Francis Adams's 1876 volume gathers familiar letters of John Adams and his wife Abigail Adams, written during the Revolution. Adams adds a memoir of Mrs. Adams, and draws on two earlier selections, the first of which ran through four editions in eight years.

The letters run between husband and wife through the years of the struggle, mixing public news with home cares, money, health, and hope. Readers meet the Revolution as a family lived it, in voices that are frank, fond, and often tired, across a long and hard war. Adams notes that the first series pleased the public, while the second sold more slowly, till both ran out.
7176-a-letter-to-a-hindu:
Leo Tolstoy wrote this letter in Russian in reply to the editor of Free Hindustan, and M. K. Gandhi's introduction tells how it passed from hand to hand before it reached him. Gandhi saw its worth at once, translated it into Gujarati, urged versions in other Indian tongues, and then had Tolstoy confirm the typed copy and grant leave to print it. The letter bears the subtitle The Subjection of India, Its Cause and Cure.

Tolstoy speaks straight to an Indian reader about rule from abroad and the path out of it, in the plain moral voice of his later years. Gandhi's framing makes the letter a bridge between a Russian prophet and an Indian cause, short in length but wide in aim. The volume preserves both the letter and the story of its journey into print.
a-letter-to-a-hindu:
Leo Tolstoy wrote A Letter to a Hindu as a reply to the editor of the journal Free Hindustan, and the hosted edition carries an introduction by M. K. Gandhi, who championed the letter in India. Its subtitle states the theme plainly: the subjection of India, its cause and its cure. Tolstoy, an old soldier turned Christian thinker, addresses Indians who hoped to end British rule.

He argues that India was not conquered by English strength so much as surrendered by Indian cooperation with violence, commerce, and military service. Against assassination and armed revolt he sets the law of love and non-resistance to evil, borne through self-suffering. Gandhi's introduction explains why he thought the letter worth translating and spreading, and it became a seed text for nonviolent resistance.
britannica-1911-boisgobey-fortune-du:
Fortuné du Boisgobey (1824–1891), whose true surname was Castille, was a French writer of popular crime tales. Born at Granville in Manche, he served in the army pay office in Algeria from 1844 to 1848 and travelled in the East. His first story appeared in the Petit journal in 1868.

With Le Forçat colonel (1872) he became a leading serial writer, and his police stories sold hugely and were widely translated into English. The entry ranks them below Émile Gaboriau's for believability, though the two names are usually linked. Titles listed run from Les Mystères du nouveau Paris (1876) to La Main froide (1889), with tales of the Terror and of Constantinople among them.
britannica-1911-bondu:
Bondu is a French protectorate in West Africa, dependent on Senegal, lying between the Faleme river and the upper Gambia. The land is a high plateau with hills in the south and centre. Those hills are barren and thinly wooded, but the low ground is fertile and rich in baobab, tamarind, and fruit trees.

Streams called marigots rush in the rains and stand empty in the dry season. The people are mostly Fula, trade is largely in Mandingo hands, and law and religion are Mahommedan, loosely kept. Mungo Park crossed Bondu in 1795, the first European traveller there, and paid heavily to its prince. Major Gray followed in 1818, when the royal town had moved from Fatteconda to Bulibani, a walled place of about 3000 people.
britannica-1911-eridu:
Eridu was one of the oldest religious centres of the Sumerians, called in Babylonian records the “city of the deep.” Its special god was Ea, god of the sea and of wisdom. The weight given to Ea in Babylonian and Assyrian incantation texts suggests that many magical writings trace back to his temple at Eridu. The entry adds that this side of Babylonian religion began there, and that old myths, above all that of Adapa, point the same way.

For all its religious weight, Eridu shows no sign of political rule in Babylonia, and it never held mastery there. Its site was found by J. E. Taylor in 1854 at the ruin called Abu-Shahrein, south-west of Ur. The entry reckons the city may have been founded as early as the seventh millennium B.C.
britannica-1911-fresnoy-charles-alphonse:
Charles Alphonse du Fresnoy (1611-1665), French painter and writer on art, was born in Paris, son of an apothecary. Meant for medicine and well schooled in Latin and Greek, he chose painting instead. He learned design under Perrier and Vouet. At twenty-one he went to Rome with no money and drew ruins to live.

In Rome he met his old fellow-student Mignard again and studied Raphael and the antique. He went on to Venice in 1633 and returned to France only in 1656. His own pictures are few, correct in drawing but wanting fire. He is remembered for his Latin poem De arte graphica, written in Italy. It is a treatise in verse on the practice of painting. Mignard published it, and Dryden later rendered it in English prose. The hosted file also holds neighbouring entries.
britannica-1911-katmandu:
Katmandu is the capital of the state of Nepal, set on the bank of the Vishnumati river where it meets the Baghmati. The town is said to have been founded about 723. Its people are put at 70,000, living in 5000 houses of brick, most of them two to four storeys high. Many houses have large wooden windows or balconies that jut out, richly carved.

The maharaja's palace, a huge, rambling, ungainly building, stands in the centre of the town, which also holds many temples. One temple, a wooden building in the centre, gives the town its name, since kat means wood. The streets are very narrow, and the whole town is judged very dirty. A British resident is stationed about a mile north of the town. The entry is a short gazetteer sketch: site, founding, houses, palace, temples, and the name itself.
doe-osti-2588108-multimodal-ligand-non-i:
Alan Heyduk of the University of California, Irvine, wrote this final technical report for Department of Energy award DE-SC0021121, dated September 11, 2025. The project ran from September 2020 through August 2024. Its subject is ligand non-innocence: ligands around a metal that do chemistry themselves, storing and releasing electrons and hydrogen atoms so the metal does not have to do every step alone.

Heyduk's team built new aminophenolate complexes of palladium, nickel, and platinum, then benchmarked how each transfers electrons, protons, hydrogen atoms, and hydrides. The summary is blunt about the lesson: charge and electronic matching between ligands decide whether two-electron hydride transfer wins over one-electron paths. A platinum catecholate complex did abstract hydride from formate, releasing carbon dioxide. Catalysis followed: one platinum complex oxidized secondary alcohols to aldehydes with oxygen as the oxidant, reaching turnover numbers as high as 650 without decomposing.
doe-osti-3011089-coal-derived-graphene-m:
Graphene materials made from coal char are scaled toward industrial use in the final report for award DE-FE0032274. Patrick Johnson of Iowa State University led the project with the University of Wyoming. Powder River Basin coal is flash pyrolysed in two passes. The first runs at 300 to 500 degrees C, the second at 700 to 1000 degrees C. Char devolatilisation reaches 38.4 percent and then 81.1 percent. A Wyoming semi works plant using six tons of raw coal per day is under construction.

The char feeds graphene oxide made by a nitric acid route, reduced graphene oxide, and hard carbons. Hard carbon anodes with 0.38 nanometre interlayer spacing suited sodium storage better than 0.36 nanometre material. Half cells used sodium metal counters and 1 M sodium perchlorate electrolyte.
doe-osti-3016980-firmware-tampering-dete:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory report ORNL/SPR-2026/4388, by Rima Asmar Awad, Joel Asiamah, Joseph Olatt, and Sam Hollifield, dates to February 2026. It studies how to spot tampered firmware in heavy-duty vehicles by watching their internal network traffic. Trucks use the SAE J1939 protocol over a controller area network to link their electronic control units.

The team captured traffic during a firmware reflash, the process that rewrites a control unit's software. During reflashing, transport protocol messages dominate the log, each line carrying a timestamp, a network identifier, and an eight-byte payload. By decoding that traffic layer by layer, analysts can build a picture of what a clean update looks like. Fleet security teams can then flag updates that do not match. The work answers a real risk: altered truck firmware can hide emissions or safety faults.
doe-osti-3023293-engineering-anti-microb: Fungi brewing germ-fighting proteins got their DOE bioprocess deal, and this CRADA 502 scales the peptide brew. The pages detail the production results. The bio folks get their data. The deal was engineering. The brew was peptide. The 502 was CRADA.
france-parlement-aix-en-provence-france-:
This decree of the Parlement of Provence, dated the first of March 1755, survives in a rough old-type scan. The court at Aix took up a letter printed at Marseille under the name of that city's bishop, with no printer's name. The letter had already been suppressed by the local court in February.

The Parlement forbade all printers, booksellers, and peddlers to reprint, sell, or distribute the letter and its declaration. Copies were to be surrendered to the court's registry for suppression. One printed copy was ordered torn up on the palace steps by an usher.
nasa-tm-19650020354-apollo-usb-system-mu:
B Kruger at Goddard wrote this report on April 21, 1965, about a problem in the Apollo communication system. The system was the USB, or Unified S-Band, link. It carried many signals at once by phase modulation on one carrier. Mixing many signals that way can distort each of them.

Kruger lays out the multisignal phase modulation problems and their solutions. A spectrum analysis of the carrier lies behind the work, the catalog note says. Apollo crews would depend on that single link for voice, data, and ranging. Sorting out its distortion problems on paper, years before flight, was essential ground work.
nasa-tm-19700018977-configuration-of-the:
D. H. Fairfield and N. F. Ness of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this preprint in May 1970. It studies the shape of Earth's magnetic tail during substorms. The tail is the long stretch of Earth's field blown away from the Sun, and substorms are sudden bursts of activity in that region.

The authors extend earlier comparisons between tail measurements and ground records from the auroral zone. Those comparisons had hinted that the tail's shape changes sharply during a substorm. Fairfield and Ness use vector field readings from the IMP 4 spacecraft to test that link. They then discuss what the changes mean for the many substorm effects seen on the ground and in space.
nasa-tm-19700027268-equatorial-scintilla:
NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center issued this preprint in June 1970. It reports radio scintillations near the equator that were met during support of the Apollo 13 mission. The events were logged from March 30 to April 18, 1970. Scintillation is a rapid fading and flutter of a radio signal passing through disturbed upper air.

The records come through the ATS 1 satellite link watched from ground stations during the flight. Signal level charts track the link day by day at Mojave, Rosman, and Iwo Jima. A cumulative chart gathers how the signal levels spread across the whole period. Conclusions and recommendations close the report, with one earlier record from Lima, Peru, kept for comparison.
podcast-dannyjones-t9Xsj_7ULDU:
YouTube prank star Jack Tenney of Joogsquad joins Danny Jones for KONCRETE number 6. Forest gives him a grand intro as a world-renowned wild man. Tenney is also brother to famed gamer Tfue.

The group jokes that Tenney serves as his dad's conscience and nemesis. Talk covers pranks, family fame, and life on camera. Tenney explains how stunts built a huge young audience. Jones keeps the tone light and fast. The episode is an early record of Florida's prank scene, told by one of its loudest young names. The family ties add warmth to the pranks.
podcast-joerogan-XMK1KEk5OdU:
Defector Yeonmi Park tells Rogan, in a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience, about escaping North Korea. Park fled as a teenager across a frozen river into China, then faced years of danger before reaching the free world. Her memoir made her one of the best-known defectors alive.

She describes hunger under the regime, the fear that governed daily life, and what freedom felt like once she reached it. Rogan asks about the parts of her story that draw attacks and doubt. The segment is a gripping first-hand account of a closed country, told by someone who paid full price to leave it.
